newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN deals double blow to Cambodia's Hun Sen.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN deals double blow to Cambodia's Hun Sen.

text.p: ASEAN postponed Cambodia's entry into the regional grouping on Thursday and said it still recognised Prince Norodom Ranariddh as co-premier despite his overthrow by rival Hun Sen last weekend.

The Association of South East Asian Nations said after an emergency meeting in the Malaysian capital that it would delay accepting Cambodia, scheduled to join along with Burma and Laos during an annual meeting later this month. "ASEAN will continue to regard Ranariddh as co-premier of Cambodia," foreign ministers from the seven-member grouping said after the meeting.

Their statement reiterated ASEAN's long-stated policy of not interfering in a neighbouring country's internal affairs, but said the use of force in the feud between Hun Sen and Ranariddh made it necessary to delay Cambodia's admission. There was no immediate response from Phnom Penh, where Hun Sen had earlier denied he had launched a coup d'etat and warned the international community to stay out of Cambodia's affairs. "ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."

At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded when his troops took control of Phnom Penh in two days of fighting at the weekend. Ranariddh left for France on the eve of the fighting. Hun Sen accused Ranariddh of provoking his own overthrow, echoing a foreign ministry white paper obtained earlier on Thursday which said Ranariddh has destabilised Cambodia by building up his own army and con ducting secret talks with the reviled Khmer Rouge. "It is not a coup d'etat. If I made a coup d'etat I would change the monarchy to a republic, suspend the constitution and arrest FUNCINPEC ministers, but everything is still the same," he told reporters, referring to Ranariddh's royalist political party.

ASEAN, which groups Indonesia, Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, said Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas and his Philippines counterpart Domingo Siazon would go to Beijing for talks with Cambodia's head of state, King Norodom Sihanouk, on ways to resolve the crisis.
From Paris Ranariddh called for talks, and his supporters vowed to set up an alternative government in northwest Cambodia, but analysts said he had little chance of fighting his way back to power.
Ranariddh was due to see U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan later on Thursday.

The two Cambodian armies agreed to a ceasefire in the west late on Wednesday after forces loyal to Sihanouk failed to enlist the support of former Khmer Rouge guerrillas, Thai army and rebel sources said in neighbouring Thailand. The Cambodian capital was tense on Thursday as foreigners scrambled to leave and supporters of Ranariddh's party were either fleeing or falling in line with the new regime.
A military official loyal to Hun Sen told Reuters from Battambang, the country's second city, on Thursday the situation was quiet.
In Phnom Penh the government said it would fly diplomats and journalists to Battambang and Siem Reap so that they could assess the situation.
